Nigerian companies may face increased regulatory scrutiny and reporting costs as new tax laws, revised accounting standards and mandatory sustainability disclosures reshape corporate compliance requirements. Ernst & Young has warned that businesses must strengthen their tax management, financial reporting and internal control systems to avoid regulatory breaches and protect investor confidence. The firm said audit committees should take a more active role in overseeing compliance, ensuring that companies identify potential liabilities and address reporting gaps before they attract regulatory sanctions. The warning was issued at the 2026 Audit Committee Transformation Summit organised by EY in Lagos on Wednesday. EY West Africa’s Partner, International Tax and Regulations, Adesope Okoh, said companies could no longer treat tax management as a routine compliance function, stressing that it should form part of strategic decisions at board level. Okoh said businesses should also evaluate the tax implications of investment decisions and changes to their business models rather than wait for regulators to uncover compliance weaknesses. She added that Nigeria’s new tax framework would require companies to continually review their internal processes as supplementary regulations and further changes emerge. On financial reporting, EY Ghana Country Manager, Emmanuel Adekahlor, urged companies to begin implementing changes required under the International Financial Reporting Standard 18, which takes effect in 2027. EY urges Nigerian firms to prepare for new tax, reporting rules Nigeria’s economic reforms require ethical accountants — ICAN EY summit set to examine emerging reporting risks He said organisations needed to identify gaps between their existing accounting practices and the new standard, particularly in their chart of accounts, information systems, internal controls and reporting procedures. Adekahlor advised audit committees to demand regular progress reports from management and involve external auditors early to minimise disruptions during the transition. He also highlighted the need to assess how IFRS 18 would affect comparative financial statements, particularly for companies preparing interim reports. On sustainability disclosures, EY executives said businesses needed reliable systems for collecting and verifying information on climate-related risks and other environmental, social and governance issues. They urged audit committees to ensure that companies had adequate data infrastructure, skilled personnel and governance frameworks to support credible disclosures and guard against greenwashing. Meanwhile, EY Associate Partner, Strategy and Transactions, Olayinka Oyetunji, identified rising debt-servicing costs, insecurity and election-related uncertainty as downside risks to Nigeria’s economic growth outlook. She projected that approximately 43 per cent of government revenue would be spent on debt servicing in 2026, leaving fewer resources for infrastructure and economic development. Oyetunji also said foreign portfolio investment accounted for about 88 per cent of Nigeria’s capital importation, underscoring the need to attract more sustainable foreign direct investment. She advised corporate boards to strengthen supply-chain resilience, diversify energy sources and improve liquidity management to withstand economic uncertainty. Odinaka Anudu
